Compute surprise and entropy, build a Huffman code, and measure the excess cost of a wrong model.

## Part A · Worksheet (~40 min, pen and paper)

### Problem 1 — Entropy ⭐

Compute entropy of $(.4,.2,.15,.15,.1)$ in bits.

### Problem 2 — Kraft ⭐

Check whether lengths $(1,3,3,3,3)$ form a complete binary prefix tree.

### Problem 3 — Huffman ⭐⭐

Run the Huffman merges for weights $(40,20,15,15,10)$, listing the combined weight at each step.

### Problem 4 — Cross-entropy ⭐⭐

For $p=(.75,.2,.05)$ and $q=(.45,.35,.2)$, compute $H(p)$, $H(p,q)$, and KL.

### Problem 5 — Perplexity ⭐

Convert 2.5 bits/symbol and 2.5 nats/symbol to their matching perplexities.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solutions — open only after attempting everything

**1.** $H=-\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i \approx 2.146$ bits, just under the $\log_2 5 \approx 2.322$ of a uniform five-symbol source.

**2.** $1/2+4/8=1$, so it exactly fills a binary tree.

**3.** Merge $10+15$, $15+20$, $25+35$, then $40+60$ (ties may change codewords, not expected length). The resulting depths $(1,3,3,3,3)$ are exactly Problem 2's lengths; average length $2.2$ bits against entropy $\approx 2.146$.

**4.** $H(p)\approx.992$, $H(p,q)\approx 1.283$, so KL $=H(p,q)-H(p)\approx.291$ bits — the price of coding $p$ with a code built for $q$.

**5.** Perplexity exponentiates in the matching base: $2^{2.5}\approx 5.657$ and $e^{2.5}\approx 12.182$.
:::
